label: CRD, RBD and Latin Square — unseen mastery test

items.stem: Which design assigns treatments to all experimental units completely at random without a planned block factor?
items.explanation: A completely randomised design uses unrestricted random allocation and has no explicit block source in its standard ANOVA.

items.stem: In a complete RBD, each block contains:
items.explanation: A complete block contains all a treatments once, with treatment positions randomised within that block.

items.stem: A standard Latin square with p treatments has:
options: p rows, p columns and p treatments
items.explanation: A p×p Latin square uses p treatments, each appearing once in every row and column.

items.stem: The two blocking factors in a Latin square are conventionally called:
items.explanation: Rows and columns represent two nuisance directions; treatment is the scientific factor of interest.

items.stem: Which design is most directly suited to one known nuisance grouping such as operator or batch?
items.explanation: A complete RBD uses one block factor; every block contains all treatments.

items.stem: Randomisation in a Latin square must:
options: Preserve one occurrence of each treatment in every row and column
items.explanation: Randomisation must preserve the Latin property, usually by permitted row, column and treatment permutations.

items.stem: A complete RBD has 4 treatments and 5 blocks. What is its error df?
items.explanation: Error df=(a−1)(b−1)=3×4=12. This is a direct application of the design definition and its degrees-of-freedom identity.

items.stem: A 5×5 Latin square has how many total degrees of freedom?
items.explanation: There are 25 observations, so total df=25−1=24.
items.check: There are 25 observations, so total df=25−1=24.

items.stem: For a 4×4 Latin square, calculate error df.
items.explanation: For p=4, error df=(p−1)(p−2)=3×2=6. This is a direct application of the design definition and its degrees-of-freedom identity.

items.stem: A complete RBD has 3 treatments and 4 blocks. Total df are:
items.explanation: N=12, so total df=N−1=11. This is a direct application of the design definition and its degrees-of-freedom identity.

items.stem: Which statements describe a complete RBD?
items.explanation: Statements A, B and D are true. A complete RBD has one block factor, and each block contains every treatment once.
statements: Every block contains every treatment once.
Treatments are randomised within each block.
There are two blocking factors by definition.

B.why: Randomisation is carried out within each block.

C.why: An RBD has one block factor; two blocking factors are used in a Latin square.

D.why: There are a treatments in each of b blocks, so N=ab.

items.stem: In a Latin square, treatment SS is calculated from treatment totals Tₖ as:
items.explanation: Each treatment appears p times, so the correction denominator for each squared treatment total is p.

items.stem: A Latin square has p=6. What is the error df?
items.explanation: Error df=(p−1)(p−2)=5×4=20. This is a direct application of the design definition and its degrees-of-freedom identity.

items.stem: Which statements are correct for a standard Latin square?
items.explanation: A, B and C are true. With one observation per cell, treatment-by-row interaction is not separately estimable from error.
statements: There are p treatments, p rows and p columns.
Each treatment occurs once in every row.
Each treatment occurs once in every column.
Treatment-by-row interaction is separately estimated with one observation per cell.

A.why: The layout is p by p with p treatments.

B.why: Each row contains every treatment exactly once.

C.why: Each column contains every treatment exactly once.

D.why: With one observation per cell, interaction cannot be separated from error.

items.stem: In the 3×3 worked Latin square, treatment totals are 29, 34 and 33. What is treatment SS?
items.explanation: SS treatment=(29²+34²+33²)/3−1024=14/3. This is a direct application of the design definition and its degrees-of-freedom identity.

items.stem: A study has two crossed nuisance directions, each with four levels, and four treatments. Which layout can control both directions while balancing each treatment across them?
items.explanation: A 4×4 Latin square has four treatments and blocks in two directions, with each treatment once in each row and column.

items.stem: In the worked 3×3 Latin square, total SS=20, row SS=8/3, column SS=8 and treatment SS=14/3. Find error SS.
items.explanation: Error SS=20−8/3−8−14/3=14/3. This is a direct application of the design definition and its degrees-of-freedom identity.

items.stem: Which limitations apply to the ordinary Latin square analysis?
items.explanation: A, B and D are true. With one observation per cell, the interactions cannot be separately estimated from residual error.
statements: The number of treatments, rows and columns must be equal.
The standard model assumes additive row, column and treatment effects.
Treatment-by-row and treatment-by-column interactions are separately estimated with one observation per cell.

A.why: The standard Latin square is p×p with p treatments.

B.why: The standard analysis uses an additive model.

C.why: One observation per cell does not allow those interactions to be separated from residual error.

D.why: Subtract three sets of p−1 df from p²−1 total df.

items.stem: A complete RBD has treatment SS=25/2 and error SS=5/6, with 3 treatments and 4 blocks. Calculate treatment F.
items.explanation: Treatment df=2; error df=6. MS treatment=25/4; MS error=5/36; F=(25/4)/(5/36)=45.
items.check: Treatment df=2; error df=6. MS treatment=25/4; MS error=5/36; F=(25/4)/(5/36)=45.

items.stem: Why can a Latin square be inefficient despite controlling two nuisance directions?
options: It always has zero error df
Its equal-level layout and additivity restrictions may not fit the experiment, and error df can be small
items.explanation: The Latin square is restrictive and may leave few residual degrees of freedom; it is useful only when the two block directions are meaningful.
